evaluations.evidence: create a new game by entering a name and an optional description
evaluations.rationale: The action and required fields are clear and do not allow materially different interpretations.

evaluations.evidence: invite estimators by giving them a URL where they can access the game
evaluations.rationale: Inviting via sharing an access URL is a single clear mechanism; no materially different meaning is implied.

evaluations.evidence: start a round by entering an item in a single multi-line text field
evaluations.rationale: Specifies the input method (single multi-line text field) and object (item) sufficiently for one interpretation.

evaluations.evidence: see all items we try to estimate this session
evaluations.rationale: ‘Items’ are consistently used across the backlog as the units being estimated; no competing interpretation is introduced here.

evaluations.evidence: select an item to be estimated or re-estimated
evaluations.rationale: Selecting an item for (re-)estimation is clear in the planning poker context and aligns with other stories.

evaluations.evidence: add an item to the list of items to be estimated
evaluations.rationale: The operation (add) and target (list of items to be estimated) are clear; minor typo does not create multiple interpretations.

evaluations.evidence: edit an item in the list of items to be estimated
evaluations.rationale: Editing an item is a clear action; while the editable fields are not enumerated, it does not create materially different interpretations of the requirement.

evaluations.evidence: delete an item from the list of items to be estimated
evaluations.rationale: Deletion of an item from the estimation list is a single, clear operation.

evaluations.evidence: show all estimates immediately
evaluations.rationale: ‘Immediately’ is vague and can mean different triggers (e.g., on moderator command, after each estimate, without waiting for all estimators), leading to materially different behaviors.

evaluations.evidence: accept the average of all estimates
evaluations.rationale: ‘Average’ is ambiguous (mean vs median vs rounded mean; handling of non-numeric/special cards), yielding materially different accepted values.

evaluations.evidence: filled in automatically if all estimators show the same card
evaluations.rationale: ‘Estimate field’ is not defined (where it is, what it represents), and ‘same card’ could exclude/include special cards; this allows different implementations.

evaluations.evidence: enter the agreed-upon estimate
evaluations.rationale: Although ‘agreed-upon’ depends on team process, the requirement is simply that the moderator can input the final estimate; no materially different system behavior is implied.

evaluations.evidence: estimate a story we estimated earlier in the session again
evaluations.rationale: Re-estimating a previously estimated story within the same session is clear and consistent with other items/rounds concepts.

evaluations.evidence: import stories from a spreadsheet
evaluations.rationale: ‘Spreadsheet’ and ‘import’ are underspecified (file type/format, required columns, mapping rules), enabling materially different interpretations of what must be supported.

evaluations.evidence: copy/paste stories from a spreadsheet
evaluations.rationale: Copy/paste source format and parsing rules are unclear (e.g., delimiter, multi-line cells, column mapping), leading to different functional interpretations.

evaluations.evidence: browse through previous games
evaluations.rationale: Browsing previous games is a clear capability; it does not hinge on a vague term that changes required behavior materially.

evaluations.evidence: view a transcript of a game
evaluations.rationale: ‘Transcript’ is not defined (what events/data it includes—chat, rounds, timestamps, participants, changes), allowing materially different outputs.

evaluations.evidence: export a transcript of a game as a HTML file
evaluations.rationale: Depends on the undefined scope of ‘transcript’ (what content is exported), so the requirement can be interpreted in materially different ways.

evaluations.evidence: export a transcript of a game as a CSV file
evaluations.rationale: CSV structure is ambiguous without defining transcript contents and column schema; multiple materially different exports are possible.

evaluations.evidence: delete a game, so that stories and estimates for this game are no longer stored
evaluations.rationale: Deletion target and intended effect (stories and estimates no longer stored) are clear enough for a single interpretation.

evaluations.evidence: create an account ... entering my name, email address, a password and a username
evaluations.rationale: Required fields are explicitly listed; no materially different interpretation is suggested.

evaluations.evidence: log in using my account name and password
evaluations.rationale: ‘Account name’ is ambiguous relative to PP-021 which distinguishes email address and username; it could mean username or email, leading to different login requirements.

evaluations.evidence: change my account details
evaluations.rationale: ‘Account details’ is vague (which fields: name, email, username, password, etc.), enabling materially different scopes of change functionality.

evaluations.evidence: delete my account, so that account information and games are no longer stored
evaluations.rationale: The action (delete account) and intended data removal scope are stated; no key term invites multiple interpretations.

evaluations.evidence: see dates and times in my local timezone
evaluations.rationale: ‘Local timezone’ is ambiguous (browser-detected vs profile setting vs OS; handling travel), leading to different functional interpretations.

evaluations.evidence: get a password reminder by email
evaluations.rationale: ‘Password reminder’ is ambiguous (sending the existing password vs reset link vs temporary password), which are materially different security/functional behaviors.

evaluations.evidence: select whether to have the team estimate with {0, 1/2, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, etc.} or {0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, etc.}
evaluations.rationale: The two alternative card sets are explicitly enumerated and named; the choice is clear.

evaluations.evidence: invite up to 15 estimators
evaluations.rationale: The limit (15) and action (invite) are clear; no materially different interpretation is implied.

evaluations.evidence: join a game by entering my name on the page I received the URL for
evaluations.rationale: Joining via the provided URL and entering a name is a clear flow with no ambiguous terms.

evaluations.evidence: see the item we're estimating
evaluations.rationale: ‘Item’ is consistently used as the unit being estimated; requirement is straightforward display.

evaluations.evidence: see all items we will try to estimate this session
evaluations.rationale: The list of items for the session is a clear concept in this backlog; no materially different interpretation arises.

evaluations.evidence: immediately see that an estimate has been given
evaluations.rationale: ‘Immediately’ is vague regarding timing/trigger (real-time push vs refresh/polling; after selection vs after submission), leading to different requirements.

evaluations.evidence: be shown all estimates at the same time after all estimators have given their estimate
evaluations.rationale: The reveal condition (after all have estimated) and simultaneous display are clearly stated.

evaluations.evidence: change my estimate up until the last person selects a card and all are shown
evaluations.rationale: The cutoff event is ambiguous: ‘last person selects a card’ vs ‘all are shown’ could be different moments depending on reveal mechanics, yielding different allowed change windows.

evaluations.evidence: see each estimator's prior estimates for the story being estimated
evaluations.rationale: ‘Prior estimates’ is ambiguous (earlier rounds in same game vs previous games vs earlier attempts at same story), leading to materially different data scope.

evaluations.evidence: see who gave what estimates during the current round
evaluations.rationale: Scope (‘current round’) and information (‘who’ and ‘what estimates’) are clear.

evaluations.evidence: be able start a two-minute countdown timer
evaluations.rationale: Starting a timer is clear, but it is ambiguous who is allowed (‘participant’ could include estimators and moderator) and whether multiple timers/overrides are possible; these lead to different behaviors.

evaluations.evidence: timer reset itself as soon as we all play an estimate
evaluations.rationale: ‘We all play an estimate’ is ambiguous (all participants vs all estimators; what counts as ‘play’), affecting when reset occurs.

evaluations.evidence: scroll back through the stories and estimates from prior rounds
evaluations.rationale: Prior rounds within the game/session is a clear scope; scrolling back implies viewing earlier entries without multiple interpretations.

evaluations.evidence: cards in the same order across multiple draws
evaluations.rationale: ‘Same order’ is ambiguous without defining the ordering rule (numeric ascending, custom deck order, moderator-defined) and what constitutes a ‘draw’, leading to different implementations.

evaluations.evidence: change my estimate as long as the draw has not been completed
evaluations.rationale: ‘Draw’ and ‘completed’ are not defined and could refer to different lifecycle points (last estimate submitted vs reveal vs moderator action), changing behavior materially.

evaluations.evidence: small thumbnail photo displayed near where my cards are played
evaluations.rationale: Placement (‘near where my cards are played’) and ownership (‘my’ photo vs others’ photos near their cards) are unclear, allowing materially different UI requirements.

evaluations.evidence: compliant with XHTML and CSS standards
evaluations.rationale: ‘Compliant’ and ‘standards’ are ambiguous without specifying versions/levels (e.g., XHTML 1.0 Strict vs Transitional; CSS2.1 vs CSS3), leading to different acceptance interpretations.

evaluations.evidence: list of definitions for commonly used terms
evaluations.rationale: ‘Commonly used terms’ is vague (which terms qualify, who decides), so the scope of the list can be interpreted materially differently.

evaluations.evidence: created database indexes
evaluations.rationale: Which tables/columns/queries require indexes is unspecified; ‘as fast as possible’ is also vague, allowing materially different implementations.

evaluations.evidence: function correctly in Internet Explorer 6 and 7, Firefox 1.5 and 2, and Safari 2
evaluations.rationale: Target browsers/versions are explicitly listed; ‘function correctly’ is broad but does not introduce multiple distinct interpretations beyond general compatibility.

evaluations.evidence: comply with the W3C accessibility guidelines where possible
evaluations.rationale: ‘W3C accessibility guidelines’ is underspecified (which standard/version/level) and ‘where possible’ is vague, enabling materially different interpretations.

evaluations.evidence: respond quickly to my actions
evaluations.rationale: ‘Quickly’ is subjective and can map to very different performance requirements (e.g., 100ms vs 2s).

evaluations.evidence: be able to use Unicode
evaluations.rationale: ‘Use Unicode’ is ambiguous (UI input only, storage, sorting, export, URLs, full UTF-8 end-to-end), leading to materially different requirements.

evaluations.evidence: see sensible and predictable URLs
evaluations.rationale: ‘Sensible’ and ‘predictable’ are subjective and can be interpreted in multiple materially different URL schemes.

evaluations.evidence: nice error pages when something goes wrong
evaluations.rationale: ‘Nice’ and ‘something goes wrong’ are vague (which errors, what content/design), allowing materially different implementations.

evaluations.evidence: stored in a non-identifiable way
evaluations.rationale: ‘Non-identifiable’ is ambiguous without defining anonymization/pseudonymization requirements and what identifiers must be removed, leading to materially different data handling.

evaluations.evidence: see some metrics on use of the game
evaluations.rationale: ‘Some metrics’ is vague (which metrics, time range, granularity), enabling materially different interpretations of what must be provided.
